Our editorial process produces two outputs: i) public reviews designed to be posted alongside the preprint for the benefit of readers; ii) feedback on the manuscript for the authors, including requests for revisions, shown below. We also include an acceptance summary that explains what the editors found interesting or important about the work.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Slow fluctuations in ongoing brain activity decrease in amplitude with ageing yet their impact on task-related evoked responses is dissociable from behaviour" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 3 peer reviewers, including Redmond G O'Connell as the Reviewing Editor and Reviewer #1, and the evaluation has been overseen by Joshua Gold as the Senior Editor. The following individual involved in review of your submission has agreed to reveal their identity: Marieke Schölvinck (Reviewer #3).

The reviewers have discussed their reviews with one another, and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this to help you prepare a revised submission.

Essential revisions:

1) The authors should provide more detailed behavioural results including false alarms and miss rates.

2) The authors should use more cautious language when discussing the strength and statistical significance of their results in a manner proportionate to the statistical power of this study.

3) In addition to controlling for their influence in the statistical models, the authors should report the degree to which the observed slow EEG/pupil fluctuations correlate with RT variability.

4) The authors should consider the possibility that the left-focussed ERP-RT relationships in fact reflect motor preparation as opposed to the CNV.

Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

The authors report in the abstract and elsewhere that their study resolves the apparently discrepant observation that older adults have higher RT variability but lower brain signal variability. The reported analyses suggest that, after controlling for background slow oscillations, older and younger groups have equivalent levels of brain signal variability. If so, this still leaves a discrepancy – older adults have higher RT variability despite equivalent brain signal variability. The authors should address this in their Discussion. Might the answer lie in the observation that older and younger adults did not differ in their coefficients of variation?

Insufficient detail is provided on the analysis of the pupil data in the Methods section. How were pupil dilations measured? This is crucial information for the reader to be able to judge the degree to which the analyses might partly reflect variations in baseline amplitude.

The initial analyses of the relationship between CNV and RT highlight a markedly left central focus in the topography. It does not seem appropriate to me to refer to such effects as relating to the CNV which is defined by its frontocentral focus. Not all activity in the pre-target window necessarily relates to the CNV process. A notable alternative candidate process here would be motor preparation with larger amplitudes reflecting greater preparation and resulting in faster RTs. It is interesting that a more frontal focus appears in the relationship when controlling for the slow fluctuations, but I think it's important for the authors to be more careful in their use of the term CNV and to discuss alternative explanations of these effects.

I am wondering why the authors did not test for a correlation between the slow EEG/pupil rhythms and RT in their data?

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

– I felt that this was an excellent paper, but its conclusions seemed very technical. Apart from knowing that we should take aperiodic signals into account in future research, I am not sure what we have now learned about aging or behavioral variability. But perhaps that's fine.

– The behavioral part of the paper feels very underdeveloped. In the methods it is explained how accuracy was calculated, yet accuracy results are not reported. I think this is quite important, because group differences in reaction time variability can originate from different sources: i) if one group is more cautious this will result in increased variability, slower RTs and higher accuracy, ii) if one group is worse at the task this will result in increased variability, slower RTs and lower accuracy, iii) not mentioning interactions between both (becoming more cautious because performance is worse) or other explanations. The authors try to address this by analyzing SD/M, but the conclusion that "increase in reaction time variability was linked to the slowdown of the responses in the older group" is very weird because RTs are not significantly different. I would think that DDM analyses would be very informative here, but that might be taking it too far (given that this does not seem to be the main focus of the paper).

– Although the sample size is quite considerable for EEG research (and I can imagine data collection for this kind of research to be far from trivial), from a statistical power perspective having only ~36 participants per group amounts to having power to detect effects of roughly.6 (effect size), which is not very sensitive. This clearly plays in the current manuscript as there are several p=.07's (RT differences; PD differences). It is great to see that the authors do no try to interpret these (e.g. not calling the "marginally significant") but at the same time, in my reading much of these.07s are very likely an issue of statistical power (i.e., BFs would be "uninformative"). The same goes for the correlations in table 1: N=38 gives you power to detect r=.43 correlations only, so I am not sure what to make of these n.s. correlations. Also, I guess that contrary to the EEG analyses, no correction for multiple comparisons was applied here?

– P.12, lines 21 and onwards; for this result to be compelling the authors should not just show that these effects become n.s., but that there is a "significant decrease" in effect with and without the adjustment (cf. Nieuwenhuis et al., 2011, Nat Neuro).

Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

– There are a lot of figures with plots showing differences e.g. in mean reaction time, amplitude of the CNV, etc. It would be helpful to indicate significance on these plots (e.g. by an asterisk), so that one does not have to search in the text whether something is significant or not.

– In the Results, the authors describe that ongoing pupil fluctuations happen at slower time scales than EEG fluctuations, and therefore longer time periods are needed to study their dynamics. While I agree completely with this statement, I am wondering why the pupil recordings from the beginning of data acquisition are analysed, and not from during the task? Wouldn't this be possible too, since there are no visual stimuli in this task?

– The correlation between CNV amplitude fluctuations and behaviour fluctuations (Figure 3) is being described as 'robust' and 'predicted behaviour fluctuations'; however, the correlations are close to zero for both younger and older adults. I would argue for less strong wording here.

results.result: The study included 36 young adults (mean age 23±3 years) and 39 older adults (mean age 60±5 years) who performed a cued auditory go/no-go task while EEG and pupil data were recorded.
results.evaluation: Claims C22 and C23 provide clear demographic information about the study participants. The sample sizes and age distributions are explicitly stated and appropriate for the study design, supporting the methodological foundation of the work.

results.result: Older adults showed significantly higher reaction time variability compared to young adults, though mean reaction time and coefficient of variation did not differ significantly. Error patterns differed, with older adults showing more misses and cue responses but similar commission errors.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C29 present behavioral findings with appropriate statistical tests and p-values. The pattern of increased RT variability (C24, p=0.013) without proportional increases in mean RT (C25, p=0.070) or CV (C26, p=0.120) is internally consistent and well-documented with specific test statistics.

results.result: Trial-by-trial variability in CNV amplitude was decreased in older adults despite the CNV showing stronger average amplitude in this group. The topographic distributions of CNV amplitude and variability group differences were distinct, with amplitude differences strongest in left central electrodes and variability differences strongest in parieto-occipital electrodes.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C34 describe the CNV findings with supporting statistical evidence and topographic analyses shown in Figure 2. The dissociation between mean amplitude (increased in older adults) and variability (decreased in older adults) is a key finding that is well-documented with appropriate corrections for multiple comparisons.

results.result: CNV amplitude fluctuations correlated with reaction time on a trial-by-trial basis, with significant correlations in left frontocentral electrodes. This association likely reflects preparatory motor activity given the contralateral topography relative to the response hand.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C39 establish the brain-behavior relationship for CNV with appropriate within-subject correlation analyses and multiple comparison corrections (C37). The interpretation regarding motor preparation (C39) is reasonable given the lateralized topography and is supported by citations (C38), though it remains an inference.

results.result: Older adults showed significantly reduced trial-by-trial variability in pupil dilation responses despite no significant difference in mean response amplitude. Preparatory pupil dilation responses did not correlate with reaction time.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C44 present pupil findings with clear statistical support. The pattern parallels the CNV results (reduced variability without reduced mean amplitude in older adults). Statistical tests are appropriate with specific t-values and p-values provided (C42: p=0.073; C43: p<0.001; C44: p=0.505).

results.result: Ongoing EEG signals in older adults showed flatter power spectral density with reduced spectral exponent and offset, reduced alpha power in occipital channels, and increased beta power in frontal/central channels.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C51 describe spectral characteristics of ongoing EEG with statistical support shown in Figure 5. The FOOOF analysis appropriately separates aperiodic and periodic components. Multiple comparison corrections were applied, and the findings are consistent with prior literature on aging and EEG spectra.

results.result: Ongoing pupil signals in older adults showed reduced spectral exponent and offset, following a 1/f distribution with no obvious periodic peaks detected.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C55 describe pupil spectral characteristics with strong statistical support (C54: exponent t(70)=7.48, p<0.001; offset t(70)=4.17, p<0.001). The findings parallel the EEG results and extend spectral flattening observations to the pupillary system. Figure 6 provides clear visualization.

results.result: Spectral properties of ongoing signals correlated with evoked response variability across participants. Higher spectral offset and exponent were associated with higher CNV and pupil dilation variability, with the strongest correlations at low frequencies (1 Hz for EEG, 0.44 Hz for pupil).
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C62 establish the link between ongoing signal dynamics and evoked response variability through correlation analyses shown in Figure 7. The frequency-specific analyses (C60-C62) provide mechanistic insight. Multiple comparison corrections were applied to topographic analyses, strengthening the conclusions.

results.result: After adjusting for spectral exponent, offset, or slow spectral power, group differences in CNV and pupil dilation variability were markedly reduced or eliminated, indicating that reduced ongoing signal fluctuations explain the decreased evoked response variability in older adults.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C66 present the critical adjustment analyses with appropriate statistical tests showing significant interaction effects and loss of group differences after adjustment. This is a key mechanistic finding supported by repeated measures ANOVAs and post-hoc t-tests with specific p-values provided (C65, C66).

results.result: Evoked response amplitudes depended strongly on the phase of ongoing slow fluctuations at cue onset, consistent with an additive model. GLM analyses showed that CNV amplitude was modulated by time-on-task and ongoing signal phase (cosine and sine functions), while pupil responses were modulated primarily by ongoing signal phase.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C72 present GLM results with strong statistical support and high explained variance (R²: EEG 63-67%, pupil 67-73%). The use of both cosine and sine functions to capture phase effects is methodologically sound. Specific t-values and p-values are provided for all predictors, and Figure 9-10 support the phase-dependence interpretation.

results.result: Adjusting for ongoing signal fluctuations unmasked or strengthened correlations between evoked responses and reaction time, particularly for pupil responses. However, even after adjustment, evoked response variability remained significantly reduced in older adults, suggesting incomplete predictability of aperiodic fluctuations.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C76 demonstrate the importance of adjustment for revealing brain-behavior relationships with appropriate statistical comparisons (C75: paired t-test t(72)=-5.08, p<0.001). The residual group difference after adjustment (C76) is an important caveat that is appropriately acknowledged and interpreted with supporting citation.

results.result: CNV and pupil dilation responses were significantly correlated on a trial-by-trial basis, with stronger correlations when accounting for the ~500ms lag in pupil responses and after adjusting for ongoing fluctuations. Multiple regression showed that CNV and pupil responses independently contribute to reaction time variance.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C81 establish the relationship between EEG and pupil measures with appropriate within-subject correlations and multiple regression analyses. The temporal lag analysis (C78) is methodologically sound. The independent contributions to RT variance (C80-C81) are supported by model comparisons with specific R² values provided.

results.result: At baseline, the descending phase of slow EEG fluctuations in left temporal channels and larger pupil size were associated with faster reaction times.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C83 describe baseline effects on behavior with appropriate statistical analyses. The pupil size effect (C83) was confirmed to be independent of time-on-task confounds. These findings suggest that ongoing signal fluctuations can affect behavior independently of their effects on evoked responses.

results.result: The study's central finding is that slow ongoing signal fluctuations strongly modulate evoked responses in an additive manner, and reduced power in these fluctuations in older adults explains their decreased evoked response variability. Critically, these ongoing fluctuation effects on evoked responses do not impact reaction time, explaining the dissociation between reduced brain signal variability and increased behavioral variability with aging.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C7 and C84-C87 represent the study's main conclusions, which are well-supported by the comprehensive analyses presented. The additive model is supported by phase-dependence analyses, the adjustment analyses demonstrate the mechanistic link, and the lack of behavioral relevance of ongoing fluctuation effects on evoked responses is shown through correlation analyses before and after adjustment.

results.result: Adjusting for ongoing signal effects was critical to unmask links between neural responses and behavior, as well as between EEG and pupil responses, demonstrating that ongoing signal variability can mask brain-behavior associations.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C9 and C91-C92 highlight a methodological insight supported by the correlation analyses shown in Figures 11-12. The demonstration that adjustment reveals previously undetectable relationships (especially for pupil-behavior correlations) is well-documented with appropriate statistical comparisons.

results.result: The effect of ongoing fluctuations on evoked responses is best explained as purely additive, reflecting the fluctuating baseline. This interpretation is supported by the substantial increase in explained variance when including phase information and by the preservation of evoked response-behavior correlations after adjustment.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C90 present the mechanistic interpretation with support from GLM analyses (C89) showing increased explained variance with phase inclusion, and correlation analyses (C90) showing preserved brain-behavior relationships after adjustment. The interpretation is also supported by citations to prior work (C88).

results.result: The study concludes that once ongoing signal fluctuations are accounted for, evoked responses show comparable variability in young and older adults, suggesting a dissociation between ongoing brain activity (reduced variability with age) and task-related responses (no age difference in intrinsic variability). This dissociation may explain why behavioral variability increases with aging despite reduced ongoing brain signal variability.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C113 summarize well-supported findings from the adjustment analyses. However, C114 is speculative about explaining increased behavioral variability with aging. The study shows that ongoing fluctuation effects on evoked responses don't explain RT variability, but doesn't fully account for why behavioral variability increases with age, as acknowledged in the discussion. The modest RT variability increase and task-specific nature of this effect limit the generalizability of this explanation.

results.result: The introduction establishes that aging is characterized by decreased brain signal variability and increased behavioral variability, reviewing prior literature on various measures of brain signal variability and their relationship to aging.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2 and C10-C21 summarize prior literature with appropriate citations. These claims establish the context and motivation for the study. While these are primarily literature review claims rather than new findings, they are accurately represented with proper attribution to cited sources.

results.result: The discussion contextualizes findings within prior literature on pupillometry, CNV, brain connectivity, and aging effects on reaction time variability, drawing connections between the current results and established knowledge.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C111 provide literature context and interpretation with appropriate citations. These claims help situate the findings within the broader literature. C108 is appropriately identified as speculation. The discussion appropriately acknowledges task-dependent effects on age-related RT variability (C109-C111).
